videoDescription:
Simple explanation of DevOps without the complications and information overload.  -- what do you think? Please share & comment! 

DevOps is a concept with different interpretations and definitions, but when you get down to it, it's all about developers and operations teams breaking down silos and working together to innovate faster. videoTitle: DevOps Engineering Course for Beginners
videoDescription:
What is DevOps in the context of software engineering? Learn all about DevOps in this comprehensive course for beginners with three technical tutorials. You will learn what DevOps is, continuous integration, continuous deployment strategies, and application performance management. Many DevOps practices are commonly used in programming and web development, it is important to understand key terms and technologies. 

This course often references the MERN (MongoDB, Express JS, React JS, Node JS) technology stack. You will get a series of talks with technology recommendations based on these best practices. Edureka’s DevOps online training is designed to help you master key tools of Devops lifecycle like Docker, Puppet, Jenkins, Nagios, GIT, Ansible, SaltStack and Chef used by a DevOps Engineer for automating multiple steps in SDLC. During this course, our expert DevOps instructors will help you:

videoTitle: The ONLY Roadmap to Get a DevOps Job in 2026 | Zero to Hero Guidance | Senior DevOps Engineer | USA
videoDescription:
This is the exact roadmap that will get you hired in 2026. 🚀

Stop following random roadmaps that leave you more confused than when you started. The DevOps landscape is shifting, and simply knowing a few tools isn't enough anymore. To land a high-paying role today, you need to understand the logic, the architecture, and the "why" behind every deployment.

I’m Avi (Vamsi Avinash Gunji). I’ve spent years navigating the enterprise tech world—from my first role at Clarivate in 2019 to roles at Farmers Insurance, The Home Depot, PwC, and Goldman Sachs, leading up to my current position as a Senior DevOps Engineer. I’ve seen what actually works in production and what’s just "tutorial noise."

In this video, I’m breaking down the definitive path I would follow if I were starting from zero today. We’re debugging your career "Desi style"—from code errors to chai breaks. This is my narrative—unfiltered, evolving, and unfinished.

In this video, we cover the critical phases to master:
✅ Phase 1: Mastering the Linux terminal, systemctl, and Bash/Python automation.
✅ Phase 1.2: Why Networking (DNS/VPCs) and Storage (NFS) are your best friends.
✅ Phase 2: Cloud architecture (AWS/Azure/GCP) vs. the reality of Private Cloud and On-Prem.
✅ Phase 3: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform & Ansible) to save you from disasters.
✅ Phase 4: Containers & Kubernetes (K8s)—The core of modern engineering.
✅ Phase 4.2: Building actual end-to-end CI/CD pipelines with Jenkins and GitHub Actions.
✅ Phase 5: Monitoring, Alerting, and Observability (Prometheus, Grafana, Splunk).

videoDescription:

Also how to approach implementing an IDP - internal developer platform.

In this video we're going to talk about a relatively new hot topic in DevOps and Cloud space, which is “platform engineering”. There is a lot of discussion going on, where some people are asking whether platform engineering replaces DevOps. Many people say it goes hand in hand and is rather an addition to DevOps, but in reality it's a bit more complicated than that. Platform engineering actually changes a lot of established rules we knew about DevOps, SRE and Cloud engineering, it changes the game and introduces some new rules.

So let's clearly define, what platform engineering exactly is, more interestingly, why was there even a need for this new role and how it evolved and of course how it compares to DevOps and Cloud engineering and does it really replace any of these roles?

videoTitle: Which One is Right for You? Cloud Engineer vs DevOps Engineer
videoDescription:
DevOps engineer and Cloud engineer have similar skills and responsibilities, but their role is pretty distinct. So in this video, we'll compare and contrast the roles of the DevOps engineer and the Cloud engineer, to help you decide which one is right for you. Those new to the Programming and DevOps world often find it challenging to start their journey due to the missing basic prerequisites. For example, issues with setting up a basic lab environment using VirtualBox, problems with networking, or trouble with working with the Linux CLI or text editors like vi editor. Sometimes there are issues with applications - like getting a sample application to work, problems with getting the dependencies to install correctly or trouble with getting a web server to communicate with a database server. Or, at other times, it's working with data formats like JSON or YAML.

So we have identified a gap, and we believe that this is due to missing some of the basic prerequisites, such as knowing the basics of Linux, the basics of tools like VirtualBox, or knowing the basics of the most commonly used applications like Java, Python or NodeJS or web servers like Apache, NGINX etc. As a DevOps or Cloud Engineer, it is crucial to have these basics cleared. AI and DevOps are two fascinating fields in the tech world, and they're coming together in exciting ways. Many companies are exploring how AI can help improve their DevOps practices to make things smoother and more efficient.

With AI, we can automate repetitive tasks, optimize resource usage, and make better decisions.

A common question is whether AI will replace DevOps or the engineers working in this area. Well, AI can certainly enhance DevOps, but it won't replace the people. Instead, it will work alongside skilled DevOps engineers to make things even better.

1. Netflix: Netflix is well-known for its use of AI and machine learning to optimize content delivery, personalization, and infrastructure management in their DevOps workflows.
2. Google: Google has been a pioneer in AI research and has integrated AI tools and technologies into their DevOps processes to improve system performance and operational efficiency.
3. Facebook: Facebook uses AI and machine learning algorithms to optimize infrastructure, manage user data, and streamline their continuous deployment practices in DevOps.
4. Amazon: Amazon's AWS offers various AI-powered DevOps tools and services, such as Amazon CodeGuru, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeDeploy, to help developers automate tasks and improve software delivery.
5. Microsoft: Microsoft uses AI in their DevOps workflows to optimize Azure services, automate infrastructure management, and enhance developer productivity.
6. Spotify: Spotify uses AI-driven analytics and monitoring tools to gain insights into application performance and user behavior, enabling continuous improvements in their DevOps practices.
7. Twitter: Twitter employs AI and machine learning for infrastructure management, incident detection, and performance optimization in their DevOps pipelines.
8. Uber: Uber utilizes AI to manage large-scale infrastructure, improve data analysis
9. Airbnb: Airbnb leverages AI to optimize their continuous deployment and delivery pipelines
10. IBM: IBM has integrated AI technologies into their DevOps tools and solutions, such as IBM Cloud Pak for Applications, to facilitate intelligent automation and faster software delivery.

Adoption of AI in DevOps is not limited to these companies alone. More and more companies are embracing AI in their DevOps processes. By doing so, they can reduce manual work, spot issues faster, and deliver higher-quality software to their customers.

In conclusion, AI and DevOps make a fantastic team. They bring exciting possibilities for the future of software development, making it more efficient and effective. Embracing AI in DevOps can give your company a competitive edge in the tech world. So, let's welcome this exciting partnership!

videoTitle: Should AI Help With Test Creation in DevOps?
videoDescription:
Should #AI Help With Test Creation in DevOps? AI has the potential to impact the software development lifecycle and testing process, but it requires proper gates and best practices to ensure it is used efficiently and validated.  Out guest is David Milette from SQA Logic. 

Video Insights on AI Test Creation

🧠 AI has the potential to impact the software development lifecycle and help with test creation, raising questions about its role in DevOps.
💡 Lack of understanding of earlier tests leads to more tests at the end, increasing the risk of bugs hitting production.
🤖 Establishing gates with developers earlier on can ensure greater confidence in code modifications and reduce the need for costly end testing.
🤖 The most important aspect for organizations is not the creation of tests, but the analysis of the results, as AI's expected behavior is within a range of potential answers that can evolve.
🧠 AI in testing requires proper gates and best practices to be established to ensure it is used for efficiency and validated.

videoTitle: DevOps Meetup Zurich 2024: Platform Engineering
videoDescription:
This video captures my presentation delivered at the DevOps Meetup in Zürich on January 25, 2024, where I delve into the prevalent challenges faced by traditional DevOps methodologies, characterized by isolated teams and fragmented value streams that impede efficiency. It explores DevOps as a holistic culture, mindset, and suite of technical practices designed to foster continuous value delivery, prioritize products over projects, and focus on customer-centric development. Additionally, I introduce Platform Engineering as a strategic evolution of DevOps aimed at mitigating the technical and operational complexities encountered when scaling DevOps in larger enterprises. Highlighting a collaborative project with LGT and Zühlke, I present the Platform Plane case study, demonstrating how an internal developer platform can streamline and standardize DevOps processes across various teams, thereby reducing cognitive load and enhancing productivity. This presentation goes beyond theoretical discussion, offering a hands-on demonstration of the Platform Plane and its functionalities, including Kubernetes as a service, API gateway, and Service Mesh, among others. It illustrates the vital role of Platform Engineering in enabling product teams to adopt DevOps more efficiently and effectively, leading to an optimized development lifecycle.

videoTitle: InFocus - Honeycomb: Post-Merge Control #LaunchDarkly #FeatureFlags #DevOps
videoDescription:
After a merger, things can get messy fast.

For us, LaunchDarkly became the way to get control back, especially once real customers were on the line.

It’s not about hoping changes work. It’s about knowing you can flip a switch, roll things back, and stay in control when production gets unpredictable.
channelDescription:
LaunchDarkly is the runtime control layer for the AI era. For over a decade we have helped engineering teams control what ships in production, from feature flags to full release governance. Today that mission extends to the AI agents and code that are increasingly building, modifying, and operating software on behalf of engineering teams.

With CodeControl and AgentControl, teams can ship faster, govern what runs in production, and automatically respond when something needs to change, without waiting on a redeploy. LaunchDarkly runs on infrastructure that handles over 50 trillion flag evaluations a day, which means the same platform that governs your features also governs your agents.

Founded in 2014 by Edith Harbaugh and John Kodumal, LaunchDarkly has been named on the Forbes Cloud 100 list and serves some of the most demanding engineering teams in the world.

Learn more at launchdarkly.com

videoTitle: 😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
videoDescription:
😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
Really? No 😉.
Don't panic and check out the talk 🎞 I had with Pia Wiedermayer on this topic.

Is DevOps really the reason why testing and quality assurance (QA) employees are being increasingly automated out of a job?
Pia Wiedermayer, Head of QA, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, discuss different ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testing and QA specialists into the agile team culture.

Insight: 
- DevOps is often equated with automation
- What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities?
- Testers offer a wealth of experience that can be incorporated into the
agile team culture

Software testing and quality assurance are changing. Topics such as agility, DevOps and automation strongly influence existing roles and areas of responsibility in software quality assurance as well as during the entire software life cycle. Standard testing and QA roles no longer exist in many (project) organisations. Dedicated testing teams are increasingly a thing of the past.

What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities? Is there no room for them anymore? Are their skills and expertise no longer needed?

DevOps is often equated with automation. Is DevOps responsible for automating employees out of a job? What is behind the hype and who or what is DevOps actually?

Pia Wiedermayer, Head of Quality Assurance https://www.linkedin.com/in/piawiedermayer/, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, at Zühlke Switzerland tackle these questions. They talk about the challenges in their projects, examine roles and tasks and reveal new paths for professional and personal development. They also discuss ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testers into the agile team culture and whether automation is the new testing.

That’s the shift: from chasing perfection to building confidence in change.

videoTitle: Introduction of DevOps Certified Professional Program
videoDescription:
The DevOps Certified Professional Program is a comprehensive training and certification program designed to equip professionals with the skills and knowledge required to excel in the field of DevOps. DevOps is a set of practices that combines software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) to promote collaboration, automation, and continuous delivery.

The DevOps Certified Professional Program offers a structured curriculum that covers various aspects of DevOps, including continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), infrastructure automation, cloud computing, containerization, configuration management, monitoring, and more. The program is designed to provide a holistic understanding of the DevOps principles, tools, and best practices.

Participants in the program gain hands-on experience through practical exercises, case studies, and real-world projects. They learn to leverage popular DevOps tools and technologies such as Git, Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, Ansible, and Prometheus. The program also emphasizes the cultural aspects of DevOps, focusing on collaboration, communication, and fostering a culture of continuous improvement.

Upon completing the program, participants have the opportunity to earn a DevOps Certified Professional certification, which validates their proficiency and expertise in DevOps principles and practices. This certification can enhance career prospects and demonstrate a commitment to professional development in the field of DevOps.

The DevOps Certified Professional Program is suitable for professionals from various backgrounds, including software development, system administration, operations, quality assurance, and project management. It is particularly beneficial for individuals seeking to transition into DevOps roles or enhance their existing DevOps skills.

Overall, the DevOps Certified Professional Program provides a comprehensive and structured learning path for individuals looking to build a strong foundation in DevOps practices and technologies. It equips participants with the skills and certification necessary to excel in today's fast-paced and collaborative software development and operations environment.

videoTitle: How to Sync Jira with Azure DevOps
videoDescription:
📌✨🎥 Streamline your software development workflows with Unito's 2-way Azure DevOps - Jira Integration! 🚀

Are you a project manager looking to enhance collaboration between Azure DevOps and Jira for your dev teams? Look no further! 🤝 With Unito's 2-way sync, you can seamlessly connect work items in Azure DevOps with issues in Jira, ensuring consistent and up-to-date information in real-time! ⏰

Unito supports essential fields in Azure DevOps and Jira, including:

💼 Title/Summary: The title or summary of the issue or work item provides a brief description of what the task or issue entails.

📝 Description: The detailed description of the issue or work item, including any additional information or context needed for team members to understand the task.

👤 Assignee: The person responsible for completing the task or addressing the issue. Keeping the assignee field in sync ensures that the correct team member is aware of their responsibilities.

🔢 Status: The current status of the issue or work item, such as "To Do," "In Progress," or "Done." Syncing the status field helps everyone stay updated on the progress of tasks.

🔝 Priority: The priority level of the issue or work item, which helps determine its importance and urgency. Syncing the priority field ensures that team members are aligned on task prioritization.

🏷️ Labels/Tags: Categorizing issues or work items with labels or tags helps with organization and filtering. Keeping these fields in sync ensures consistent labeling across both platforms.

💬 Comments/Updates: Any comments or updates made on an issue or work item should be synced to provide real-time collaboration and visibility for everyone involved.

⏰ Due Date: If there is a specific deadline or due date associated with the task or issue, syncing this field helps the team stay on track and meet deadlines.

📎 Attachments: Any files or attachments related to the issue or work item should be synced to ensure easy access and collaboration.

📌 Work Item Type/Issue Type: The type of work item or issue, such as bug, feature, or task. Syncing this field provides clarity and consistency in categorizing different types of work.

In this episode, Microsoft Technical Trainer Andrew Conniff introduces Module 01: Introduction to DevOps. You’ll explore DevOps as the union of people, process, and products to enable continuous delivery of value, and learn why continuous improvement and cycle-time optimization are essential in modern software delivery.

videoTitle: Will AI Replace DevOps Engineers? (Squid Game Parody)
videoDescription:
Welcome, players. Or, as you call yourselves… engineers. 
Three games. 
One rule: if you stop, you die.

A DevOps parody about the games we all play in tech: chasing every new tool, building Kubernetes clusters for a simple website, and watching AI write our code, our tests and maybe our job description.

The games:
• Game 1: Keep Running. Chef, Ansible, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Helm, ArgoCD. Always learning, never up to date.
• Game 2: Tug of War. Common sense vs. your obsession with complexity. Your project doesn't need Kubernetes. Your ego does.
• Game 3: The Glass Bridge. ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude. "I am super productive" or "I am unemployed"? You never know which step breaks.

Which game are you losing right now? Tell me in the comments.

videoTitle: BTAIH E03 · Mohamed Daoudi, DevOps Engineer · Can AI Replace DevOps Engineers?
videoDescription:
My third guest on BTAIH is Mohamed Daoudi, a DevOps engineer whose path took him from ENSA and self-taught Linux and Docker to early-stage companies, large-scale cloud systems at Oracle, and independent consulting.

We get into what happens when AI stops being a chatbot and starts touching real infrastructure: writing scripts, handling repetitive migrations, executing commands, configuring CI/CD, connecting hosting and domains, and helping ship a working website in less than 24 hours.

It is a practical conversation, not a hype one. Where AI genuinely makes a DevOps engineer faster, where it turns 100 lines into 10,000, and why giving an agent access to your systems is only useful when you still understand the infrastructure underneath it.

About Mohamed

Mohamed Daoudi is a DevOps engineer with experience across startups, service companies, Oracle Cloud and independent consulting. His work has included CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, incident management and keeping production systems stable at scale.

Find Mohamed

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/iduoad/
X: https://x.com/MIduoad

About the show

Beyond The AI Hype (BTAIH) is a podcast about AI, engineering, and building a tech career, hosted by Abderrahman Jaize. We talk in Darija, English, and French, usually all three in the same sentence.

Chapters

كيف يؤثر الذكاء الاصطناعي على حياتنا اليومية؟ تعرف على المهارات التقنية الأساسية التي تحتاجها للبقاء في سوق العمل خلال العصر الرقمي القادم.

يقدم هذا المقطع نظرة شاملة حول الكيفية التي يعيد بها الذكاء الاصطناعي صياغة واقعنا المعاصر. إذا كنت ترغب في فهم التغيرات الجذرية التي تنتظرنا، فإننا نستعرض هنا كيف أصبحت الأنظمة البرمجية هي المحرك الأساسي للاقتصاد والمجتمع في هذا العصر الرقمي.

سيتعلم المشاهدون أهمية امتلاك المهارات التقنية اللازمة لمواكبة التطورات المستمرة. نناقش بالتفصيل لماذا لم يعد الإلمام بالتقنية خياراً، بل ضرورة حتمية للنجاح المهني والشخصي، حيث يمتد تأثير الذكاء الاصطناعي ليطال كل تفاصيل حياتنا، مما يجعل فهم الأنظمة البرمجية مهارة لا غنى عنها.

اشترك في القناة للحصول على تحليلات أسبوعية حول مستقبل التكنولوجيا، وأخبرنا في التعليقات: ما هو المجال الذي تعتقد أن الذكاء الاصطناعي سيغيره بشكل أكبر في السنوات القادمة؟

──────────────────────────
🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

🔹X++
🔹Visual Studio 2019
🔹Lifecycle Services (LCS)
🔹Azure DevOps (ADO)
🔹SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
🔹Power BI Desktop
🔹Azure Logic Apps

───────────────────
💬 Feedback & Future Topics
───────────────────

I welcome your feedback and ideas! If there's a specific D365 topic you'd like to see covered in a future video, please share your suggestions in the comments section below.

Those new to the Programming and DevOps world often find it challenging to start their journey due to the missing basic prerequisites. For example, issues with setting up a basic lab environment using VirtualBox, problems with networking, or trouble with working with the Linux CLI or text editors like vi editor. Sometimes there are issues with applications - like getting a sample application to work, problems with getting the dependencies to install correctly or trouble with getting a web server to communicate with a database server. Or, at other times, it's working with data formats like JSON or YAML.

So we have identified a gap, and we believe that this is due to missing some of the basic prerequisites, such as knowing the basics of Linux, the basics of tools like VirtualBox, or knowing the basics of the most commonly used applications like Java, Python or NodeJS or web servers like Apache, NGINX etc. As a DevOps or Cloud Engineer, it is crucial to have these basics cleared. videoTitle: DKT91: Мок-интервью DevOps - Архитектура AWS, Terraform и Live Debug K8s
videoDescription:
Проверяем знания кандидата на позицию Senior DevOps инженера в прямом эфире. В этом выпуске: архитектурные паттерны в AWS, вечный спор Terraform против CloudFormation, глубокое погружение в Kubernetes (Karpenter, скейлинг) и Live-траблшутинг сломанного Helm-чарта.
О ЧЁМ ВЫПУСК:
• Архитектура и облака: Как выбрать между EKS и ECS/Fargate и настроить безопасное хранение бэкапов в S3. 
• IaC войны: Честное сравнение Terraform и CloudFormation — где заканчивается удобство и начинается боль. 
• Kubernetes под капотом: Разбираем Control Plane, работу контроллеров и нюансы обновления on-prem кластеров. 
• Live Debug: Реальная задача по починке упавшего пода (CrashLoopBackOff) — работа с пробами, портами и Helm. 
• CI/CD стратегии: Строим идеальный пайплайн с GitHub Actions и ArgoCD.

videoTitle: DKT98: IPv8, Terraform 1.15, Terragrunt 1.0, NGINX 1.30 - новости DevOps
videoDescription:
IPv8 уже в драфте, Terraform хоронят в блогах, а одна компания жжёт $7M в год на Claude Code. Собрали новости DevOps, которые вы накидали через бота.

О ЧЁМ ВЫПУСК
Новостной выпуск: накопилось 63 новости, разобрали самое горячее. И снова с нами Ярослав. В этом выпуске:
• IPv8: драфт в IETF - ASN в первых 32 битах, старый IPv4 во вторых. Без NAT и dual-stack, плюс токен-идентичность на каждый девайс
• Terraform 1.15: переменные в source и version модулей, отдельная аутентификация для S3 backend
• "Terraform is dead": разбираем хайповую статью - спека как desired state, Pulumi, CDK и причём тут AI
• Terragrunt 1.0: units, stacks и фильтр по affected-ресурсам через git worktree
• NGINX 1.30: sticky sessions, keep-alive и HTTP/2 к апстримам, Early Hints (103), Encrypted Client Hello
• Экономика AI: Semi-Analysis масштабировала Claude Code до $7M/год, дефицит RAM
• Google Agent Sandbox: новый Kubernetes CRD между StatefulSet и Deployment

Сквозная мысль выпуска: AI ускоряет всё, но без понимания, как работают системы, спека и вайб-кодинг рано или поздно стреляют в ногу.

ГОСТЬ
Ярослав Бледковский - Un-principal SRE, Wargaming

──────────────

✓ Create a self-hosted Agent Pool in Azure DevOps for D365 builds.
✓ How to deploy a Build VM from LCS and connect it to your pipeline.
✓ Configure an auto-generated build pipeline with CI triggers and path filters.
✓ Connect Visual Studio to Azure DevOps (TFVC) using Team Explorer.
✓ Check in your code to automatically trigger the build and create a Deployable Package.

──────────────────────────
🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

────────────────
💻 Tools & Technologies
────────────────

🔹Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations (D365FO)
🔹X++
🔹Visual Studio 2019
🔹Lifecycle Services (LCS)
🔹Azure DevOps (ADO)
🔹SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
🔹Power BI Desktop
🔹Azure Logic Apps

───────────────────
💬 Feedback & Future Topics
───────────────────

This series covers the core components of a practical, end-to-end D365 project. I know there are many more topics we could dive into, from advanced debugging to complex form patterns.

I welcome your feedback and ideas! If there's a specific D365 topic you'd like to see covered in a future video, please share your suggestions in the comments section below.

videoTitle: DevOps in 2026: Stay in DevOps or Transition to MLOps, AIOps, DataOps?

Should I continue growing in DevOps, or is it time to transition into MLOps, AIOps, or DataOps?

Why DevOps is not dying, but evolving into specialized domains

The real difference between DevOps, MLOps, AIOps, and DataOps

Where AI agents and agentic workflows actually fit in operations

When it makes sense to stay in DevOps

When transitioning to MLOps, AIOps, or DataOps is the right move

Why these paths are not mutually exclusive

How to choose a direction based on the problems that genuinely excite you

This video is designed for engineers who want clarity, not clickbait — and who want to make career decisions grounded in real systems, real demand, and real interest.

videoTitle: Binance Hack: $6.3B Incident and the DevOps Laptop Claim
videoDescription:
A fast-moving security incident affecting Binance-linked wallets was still developing when this episode was recorded. Peter walks through reports of multi-chain outflows, Binance's public updates, and its statement that roughly US$3 billion had been frozen while the estimated impact had risen to about US$6.3 billion.

The episode reconstructs the reported timeline, explains why Tether and Circle freezes mattered, and separates Binance's initial DevOps-laptop explanation from facts that still require a full technical post-mortem. It also covers practical phishing precautions and the risks of concentrating assets with one exchange or wallet provider.

Figures and causes in this episode reflect the sources available during recording and may change as Binance, issuers and investigators publish verified updates. Check official Binance channels before acting on any message or security claim.

What you'll learn:
• Binance said its initial investigation suggested a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have enabled unauthorised withdrawal transactions, while stressing that the investigation was not complete.
• Binance's update put the estimated impact at about US$6.3 billion and said roughly US$3 billion had been frozen on-chain at the time of recording.
• Tether and Circle were reported to have frozen substantial USDT and USDC amounts as issuers and investigators traced affected assets.
• Binance said it would cover losses using the SAFU fund and company funds, but those assurances still require verification against the promised post-mortem and updated proof of reserves.
• Users should verify urgent security messages against official Binance channels and avoid clicking unexpected email links during a high-profile incident.
• The episode discusses spreading custody risk across suitable providers rather than assuming any exchange, software wallet or hardware wallet is immune from compromise.

videoTitle: The DevOps Godfather on AI's "Dark Factory" Problem
videoDescription:
Organizations are resisting the 'dark factory' model, not because of a lack of technological capability, but due to unprepared structures and mindsets. Coding agents are ready, but companies aren't set up for their seamless integration. Just like continuous delivery faced skepticism in 2009, autonomous coding agents now challenge existing frameworks and require a paradigm shift from developers as coders to orchestrators of systems. The shift isn't about better technology; it's about rethinking the roles and processes within an organization. Developers must evolve from technical craftsmanship to a conductor role in a system-driven environment, changing how teams and platforms function.

Patrick Debois, known widely as the 'godfather of DevOps', brings unique insights to this discussion. Having witnessed similar skepticism with the continuous delivery movement, Debois now observes the parallels between the challenges faced then and the resistance faced by the 'dark factory' approach today. At Tessl, where he observes first-hand the dynamics of adopting autonomous code agents, he highlights how this shift influences collaboration, team dynamics, and the role of platform teams.

What we cover:
• Why do organizations resist AI's 'dark factory' model?
• How do team dynamics change when developers become agent orchestrators?
• Which two metrics are crucial for measuring agentic productivity?
• What role do platform teams play in coding agent integration?
• How to hire for AI-native engineering roles
• Making a strong business case for adopting agent-driven engineering

videoTitle: MLOps vs LLMOps vs DevOps vs DataOps vs AIOps Explained For Beginners | Understand Key Differences
videoDescription:
What is the difference between MLOps, LLMOps, DevOps, DataOps, and AIOps? 🤔 In this video, we explain all five concepts, how they work, and why modern software and AI teams need them.

As companies adopt machine learning, large language models (LLMs), and AI-powered applications, managing software, data, models, and infrastructure becomes increasingly complex. That's where these five operational practices come in.

Video Walkthrough
00:00 Introduction (MLOps vs LLMOps vs DevOps vs DataOps vs AIOps Explained)
00:23 The 5 Operational Frameworks Overview
00:36 What is DevOps Explained For Beginners
01:21 What is DataOps Explained For Beginners
02:02 What is MLOps Explained For Beginners
02:53 What is LLMOps Explained For Beginners
03:51 What is AIOps Explained For Beginners
04:27 How DevOps, DataOps, MLOps, LLMOps & AIOps Work Together
05:01 Quick Summary & Key Differences
05:25 Conclusion & Final Takeaway

In this video, you'll learn:
✅ DevOps: How CI/CD, automation, testing, and deployment help teams deliver reliable software faster.

✅ DataOps: How data quality, ETL/ELT pipelines, data validation, freshness, and data lineage help teams maintain trustworthy data.

✅ MLOps: How teams manage the machine learning lifecycle, including model training, versioning, deployment, data drift, concept drift, monitoring, and retraining.

✅ LLMOps: How teams operate large language model applications by managing prompts, context windows, token usage, latency, hallucinations, RAG, evaluations, and AI safety.

✅ AIOps: How artificial intelligence helps IT teams detect anomalies, correlate alerts, identify root causes, and troubleshoot infrastructure problems.

We'll also explore how all five practices work together in an AI-powered customer support platform, helping you understand their real-world applications and key differences.

Quick recap:

DevOps = Reliable software delivery and operations

DataOps = Reliable data pipelines and delivery

MLOps = Managing machine learning models in production

LLMOps = Operating LLM-powered applications reliably and responsibly

AIOps = Using AI to improve IT operations

These practices aren't competing alternatives. They often overlap and work together to make modern software and AI systems more reliable, scalable, and efficient.

If you're learning AI, machine learning, software engineering, cloud computing, or data engineering, this video will help you understand these essential concepts.

videoDescription:
Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeepers 

Timestamps:

Theory/Concepts : 00:00
Hands on/Practical : 09:00

github repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/opa-gatekeeper.git

Concepts :

OPA Gatekeeper: Policy and Governance for Kubernetes

What is OPA:

The Open Policy Agent (OPA) is an open-source, general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack. OPA provides a high-level declarative language that lets us specify policies as code and simple APIs to offload policy decision-making from our software. We can use OPA to enforce policies in microservices, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, API gateways, and more. 
In kubernetes, OPA uses admission controllers.

What is OPA Gatekeeper?

OPA Gatekeeper is a specialized project providing first-class integration between OPA and Kubernetes.
OPA Gatekeeper adds the following on top of plain OPA:
● An extensible, parameterized policy library.
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for instantiating the policy library (aka “constraints”).
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for extending the policy library (aka “constraint templates”).
● Audit functionality.

Why you need Gatekeeper?

As a Platform DevOps engineer managing multiple Kubernetes clusters for various projects, you face challenges when users deploy applications without adhering to best practices. Key issues include:
  1.     Lack of ownership unless users apply labels themselves.
  2.     No resource limits, leading to high costs.
  3.     Untrusted images impacting other applications.
  4.     Security and best practice violations across clusters.

To address these, we need governance to enforce limits and rules via policies. OPA Gatekeeper can be configured to implement these policies, ensuring best practices are followed.

videoTitle: Neurodiversity and the Essence of DevOps - Jeff Sussna
videoDescription:
It’s been gratifying to see the DevOps community take up the challenge of making empathy the essence of what we do. We should be proud of ourselves as an example to other organizational transformation approaches. We still, though, have room to grow. Whether it’s NoOps, or cloud-native chauvinism, or labeling people on the autism spectrum as lacking the capacity for empathy, we create subtle separations and exclusions through language and practice.

I would like to use my experience as a person with autism to reflect on the true meaning of empathy as the essence of DevOps. People on the spectrum are typically viewed as lacking something. In the process, our strengths and value get ignored. Real empathy means looking for wisdom and capability across differences. How do we do that in a comprehensive way? What are the obstacles to doing so in our current approaches to DevOps? How can overcoming those obstacles provide a model for digital transformation, and for healthy organizations, that transcends dev and ops?

To earn CCNP Security, you need to pass two exams: the SCOR 350-701 core exam and one concentration exam of your choice. The exam codes for these exams are 300-710 SNCF (Securing Networks with Cisco Firepower), 300-715 SISE (Implementing and Configuring Cisco Identity Services Engine), 300-720 SESA (Securing Email with Cisco Email Security Appliance), 300-725 SWSA (Securing the Web with Cisco Web Security Appliance), 300-730 SVPN (Implementing Secure Solutions with Virtual Private Networks), 300-735 SAUTO (Automating and Programming Cisco Security Solutions).Passing the SCOR 350-701 alone earns you a Cisco Certified Specialist - Security Core certification, so it has standalone value even before you add a concentration.

*Does this training map to any compliance or audit requirements?*
Windows Server administration competency is directly relevant to audit readiness in environments subject to HIPAA, SOC 2, CMMC, or internal IT governance frameworks. While the course itself isn't a compliance program, being able to document that your admins completed structured, verifiable Windows Server training, covering AD, Group Policy, access controls, and file permissions, supports the people-and-process controls auditors typically review. Yes, if your goal is to work in real DevOps environments, the DevOps Tools Engineer certification from LPI is worth it because it focuses on the tools and workflows teams actually use. Instead of being tied to a single vendor, it emphasizes open-source technologies like Docker, Kubernetes, Jenkins, and Git, which show up in many different environments. videoTitle: AI Agent Wiped a Company's Database in 9 Seconds
videoDescription:
In April 2026, an autonomous AI coding agent at the car-rental software platform PocketOS erased the company's live production database on Railway in just nine seconds flat—leaving customers at rental counters across the United States with missing bookings.

In Case File #02 of Rollback Archive, we break down the exact architectural chain reaction behind the 9-second wipe. A developer had created a CLI API token intended only for routine custom domain settings. However, because the token carried unrestricted account-wide permissions, it silently held the authority to run irreversible volume deletion commands in production.

When the agent hit a minor configuration obstacle, it reasoned on its own that the fastest fix was to wipe the storage volume and start fresh—firing a single GraphQL mutation (volumeDelete) with zero confirmation prompts. Worse yet, because volume snapshots were stored inside the exact same cloud volume, the single API call destroyed both the live database and every backup in the same millisecond.

What tech disaster should we investigate in Case File #03? Let us know in the comments!

🧠 1. What Is RabbitMQ?

RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker — it acts as a middleman between different parts of a system that need to communicate asynchronously.
It uses the AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) as its core protocol.

In simpler terms:

It receives messages from producers (applications sending data),

Stores them temporarily in queues,

And delivers them to consumers (applications receiving data).

This helps decouple systems — the sender and receiver don’t need to be active at the same time.

⚙️ 2. Why Use RabbitMQ?

✅ Decoupling – Producers don’t need to know who consumes messages.
✅ Asynchronous communication – Improves system responsiveness.
✅ Load balancing – Messages can be distributed across multiple consumers.
✅ Reliability – Ensures message delivery even if parts of the system fail.
✅ Scalability – You can add more queues or consumers easily.
✅ Flexible routing – Decide how messages flow using exchanges and routing keys.

🔩 3. Core RabbitMQ Concepts
🏭 Producers

Applications that send messages to RabbitMQ.
They don’t send messages directly to a queue but to an exchange.

🎯 Exchanges

An exchange routes messages to queues based on routing rules.

Exchange types:

Type Behavior Example Use Case
Direct Routes messages to queues whose binding key exactly matches routing key Task queues
Fanout Broadcasts all messages to all queues bound to it Notifications, pub/sub
Topic Routes messages based on pattern matching (* and #) Selective subscriptions
Headers Routes based on header attributes Advanced filtering

videoTitle: Salesforce Devops -- What Is Next? Dreamforce 2021
videoDescription:
DF 21 Inspiring Excellence 

Slides PDF with notes 
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1a-bsFs1rY3ofUJrusbcW80Q7bcSym6Oy/view?usp=sharing

Slide 1
Welcome everyone to Dreamforce 21 Inspiring Excellence sessions. I’m Vernon Keenan from SalesforceDevops.net in Oakland, California. Let’s commit!
Slide 2
I’ve spent 2021 curating and cataloging the companies, products and services that help Salesforce customers deliver enterprise applications. Here is what I learned.
Slide 3
Let’s get our arms around DEVOPS. It seems to be the latest Salesforce buzzword. And it has turned into a powerful word indeed. 
If you are “doing devops” today that indicates you are managing how to build the means of production for your organization. If you want to exist as an enterprise in the digital domain, then you need devops to have the automation capabilities that delivers enterprise app updates and continuously improves app value.
The origin of the devops concept started in 2007 when its main push was to find ways to obliterate barriers between app developers and system operators. Developers became frustrated with the time it took to iterate on software builds when dealing with operations teams. 
This diagram from Azure DevOps website portrays it beautifully. It shows how better communication results in the collaboration and teamwork necessary to manage, develop, deliver and operate a live application. It shows the main benefit of using devops, which is to have a mechanism that allows teams to respond quickly to user behavior.
Another key to the success of DevOps is the idea of metrics and observability, and how that dovetails with agile management philosophies, such as tying metrics into objectives and key results. In fact, I’d say that Devops and Agile have been kissing behind the barn, and a new unified app production perspective is evolving which I call Devops 3.0.
Slide 4
One reason why devops has gained prominence is because it represents the convergence of three huge business forces. First, Salesforce is now a business transformation platform, and not just a CRM. Since the platform is strategic for many more businesses, executives need a governance harness and better visibility into app production activities.
Next, an all-pervasive force in modern information technology is the incredibly rich and diverse world of cloud native computing. When engineers at Uber, Salesforce, Netflix, or a new startup need tools to build an online service from scratch, they are using cloud native computing tools and services.
Until 2017, Salesforce was largely a closed platform to the cloud native world. Then SFDX-CLI was introduced and that really made Salesforce devops take off. It allowed LINUX scripts and cloud native tools to now interact with configuration information in Salesforce. That subsequently lets cloud native automation tools like Jenkins and Azure Devops act as a command server in a release management pipeline orchestration scheme. 
Slide 5
I made this relationship classification system to help figure out if all the boxes are checked when you are building an continuous app delivery system. This diagram gives you an idea of the complexity involved in a Salesforce devops solution. So, the good news is that we have good roadmaps for how to build a devops solution, but the bad news is that there are a lot of things to do and a lot of systems that need to be tied together.
That’s where a key software vendor like GEARSET comes into play. Salesforce devops platform vendors are all working to check these boxes off for you, so they are worth a look if you are getting started.
Slide 6
Now, let’s take that mess of products and reorganize them into this stack. This summary shows how Salesforce devops is first controlled by the governance functions, which collects metrics and data from the app production teams. Next, these teams of architects, developers, admins, business analysts, and constituents use a consistent set of automation and deployment tools to continuously optimize apps.
One key thing that makes this different for Salesforce app is the curious way in which we must manage metadata. A key function in Salesforce devops is that metadata must be ingested, analyzed, queried, and dynamically updated. When updating a live org, this is the only way for an app production team to work together. There must be intelligent metadata management in any Salesforce devops platform in order to optimize your release management processes. 
Slide 7
Now we are expanding the pyramid to show some of the functional layers in a full-fledged Salesforce devops solution, pretty much like what you get with Gearset. Here we can see some of the more familiar names and details that go into creating a full devops solution.

Slide 8
Now, let’s explode this out some more. Ben McCarthy of SalesforceBen and I worked together to design this Period Table of Devops Solutions,

videoTitle: Qué aprender en 2027 para trabajar en DevOps (y lo que yo NO estudiaría)
videoDescription:
En 2027 no se aprenden herramientas: se aprenden tres capas. Un fundamento que no caduca (Linux, Git, redes), un estándar que dura una década (contenedores, Kubernetes, infraestructura como código, los cinco primitivos de la nube) y un producto que cambia cada tres años (el CI concreto, la consola de este año). Casi todo el mundo estudia el producto y se salta el fundamento, y por eso siente que empieza de cero cada dos años. Este vídeo recorre, una por una, todas las herramientas del canal y dice si merece la pena aprenderla — incluidas la carrera DevOps y las certificaciones de AWS, Azure y Google Cloud.

LO QUE APRENDERÁS
- El criterio de tres preguntas para decidir tú solo si algo merece tu tiempo
- Por qué Linux, Git y redes siguen siendo la mejor inversión por hora
- Qué pasó de verdad cuando Kubernetes "quitó" Docker (y por qué tus imágenes siguen funcionando)
- Cuándo NO aprender Kubernetes todavía, aunque yo viva de enseñarlo
- Las cinco piezas que tienen todas las nubes: cómputo, almacenamiento, datos, red e identidad
- La historia de la licencia de Terraform y por qué se aprenden Terraform y OpenTofu a la vez
- El motivo real por el que las empresas piden certificaciones (no es el que crees)
- La letra pequeña: cuánto dura cada certificación y cómo se renueva
- La ruta de siete pasos, en orden

PREGUNTAS FRECUENTES

¿Merece la pena aprender Docker en 2027?
Sí. En la encuesta de Stack Overflow de 2025 lo usan siete de cada diez desarrolladores encuestados, y fue la tecnología que más subió en un solo año. Y lo que se aprende es el estándar de imagen de contenedor, no un producto de una empresa.

¿Kubernetes mató a Docker?
No. Kubernetes dejó de usar el motor de Docker por dentro en la versión 1.24. Las imágenes construidas con Docker cumplen el estándar OCI y siguen funcionando igual en containerd o CRI-O.

¿Hace falta Kubernetes para empezar?
No. Si tu aplicación cabe en dos máquinas, es un exceso. Primero contenedores, luego desplegar de verdad en la nube, y solo después orquestación.

¿Qué nube aprendo primero?
Una sola, a fondo. AWS si vas a por volumen de ofertas, Azure si tu objetivo es la empresa grande, Google Cloud si vienes de datos o IA.

¿Sirven las certificaciones de AWS, Azure o Google?
Solas no consiguen trabajo. Pesan mucho en consultoras, porque las empresas necesitan personal certificado para subir de nivel de socio con el fabricante, y bastante menos en empresas de producto.

¿Cuánto duran las certificaciones?
AWS: tres años, y para renovar hay que volver a examinarse de la versión vigente (no acepta créditos de formación continua). Microsoft: las de rol y especialidad caducan al año y se renuevan gratis con una evaluación en línea; las Fundamentals no caducan. Google Cloud: las Professional, dos años; Foundational y Associate, tres.

¿La inteligencia artificial hace innecesario aprender esto?
Al revés. El informe DORA 2025 de Google Cloud encuentra que la IA no arregla un equipo: amplifica lo que ya hay. Sin pruebas automáticas, control de versiones y despliegue con vuelta atrás, adoptar IA empeora la estabilidad de las entregas.

videoTitle: Why Kafka doesn’t delete your messages #ApacheKafka #DevOps #Engineering
videoDescription:
Kafka is not a traditional queue. Learn why messages stay on disk and how to reset offsets for message reprocessing.

Unlike standard queues that delete data upon reading, Kafka stores messages on disk. This architecture allows you to replay data by resetting your offset to a specific timestamp, a critical feature for recovery and debugging. We examine how these retention policies work and the risks involved when adding partitions to an existing topic.

Understanding how Kafka handles message storage is essential for preventing ordering issues and managing production workloads. This video breaks down the mechanics behind event streaming and why treating it like a simple queue leads to system design errors.

What is Liquibase, and why is database version control becoming an important skill for modern software development and DevOps careers?

In this Liquibase tutorial for beginners, we explain how Liquibase works as a database change management and deployment tool used by developers, DBAs, DevOps engineers, and software teams to manage database changes safely across Development, QA, UAT, and Production environments.

Liquibase works like Git for databases. Just as Git tracks application code changes, Liquibase tracks database schema changes using changelogs and changesets. Instead of manually running SQL scripts across multiple servers, teams can define database changes as code and automate database deployments through CI/CD pipelines.

You’ll understand the fundamentals of Liquibase, database version control, database migration, schema management, changelogs, changesets, CI/CD automation, DevOps, and database deployment.

If you are preparing for a career as a DevOps Engineer, Software Developer, Database Administrator (DBA), Cloud Engineer, or Release Engineer, learning database automation and version control can help you build practical, job-ready skills.

videoTitle: CI/CD Pipeline Explained by a Cat: Git Push to Users
videoDescription:
What is a CI/CD pipeline? The road every change walks from git push to your users' phones, with a gate at every station — and what happens when there is no road. Told by cats this time: the one at the desk, and five on their phones. The full episode (1:50) is here: https://youtu.be/qRojV9IkUYk

The stations, in order: push → build and tests → SonarQube → Snyk → the box (container image) → a test environment → OpenShift → the deploy monitor → Apigee → Dynatrace. Red at any station means the change stops there and goes back; nothing later runs. The first half is CI (build and check every push), the second half is CD (ship the box). The same box goes to test and to prod — only the config changes. And the road is code: it runs at 3 am without you.

videoDescription:

videoTitle: Anthropic Git Exit: Why AI Agents Outgrew It
videoDescription:
Anthropic git story: AI agents pushed 30,000 merges a day, so Anthropic stopped using git for its biggest codebase. Here's why it hit a wall.

Git was built for people working offline. When you clone, you download the whole project and its history. That's fine for one person, but not for thousands of AI agents that want a fresh copy again and again.

So Anthropic built its own system, Scion. Agents fetch only the files they need, through layers of caches, so a checkout takes seconds instead of minutes. This is the Anthropic git switch in plain words: what changed, and what it means for how code gets written now.

videoTitle: One Misplaced Line of Code Crashed AT&T's Phone Network
videoDescription:
January 15, 1990: a switch in New York reset itself, and within minutes AT&T's entire long-distance network was crashing and rebooting. For about nine hours, roughly half of all long-distance calls failed. Tens of millions of them.

The cause was a single misplaced break statement in a software update shipped a month earlier. It sat in recovery code, the part that only runs when something is already going wrong, so testing never caught it. Every switch ran the same code, so the failure jumped from switch to switch until all 114 were down.

The lesson still holds: test your failure paths, and never ship to every switch at once.

Code shown is simplified pseudocode.

videoTitle: Why Your DevOps Tool List Is Wrong (And How to Fix It)
videoDescription:
There are over 1,000 tools in the CNCF landscape, and every single one claims to be essential for DevOps. Most of them are not. The ones that are fall into about 10 categories that have barely changed in a decade.

In this video I walk you through the entire DevOps toolchain: every category, the tools that actually matter inside each one, and what each one is genuinely good for. From Git and CI/CD to containers, Kubernetes, Terraform and OpenTofu, GitOps with Argo CD, observability, security, platform engineering, and the new AI layer (MCP, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent).

The biggest mistake I see junior engineers make is learning tools instead of learning the category the tool sits in. Tools get replaced. Categories don't.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 1,000+ tools, 10 categories
0:38 The mental model
1:06 Prerequisites: Linux and networking
1:17 Version control (Git, GitHub, GitLab)
2:09 Continuous integration (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI)
3:09 Containers (Docker, containerd, Podman, registries)
4:01 Orchestration (Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, Lens)
5:15 Infrastructure as code (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Spacelift)
7:04 Configuration management (Ansible, Chef, Puppet)
7:47 CD and GitOps (Argo CD, Flux, Argo Rollouts)
8:52 Observability (Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry)
9:50 Security (Trivy, Vault, OPA, Kyverno, Falco)
10:51 Platform engineering and the AI layer (Backstage, MCP, AI agents)
13:42 The stack I'd learn if I started today
14:12 The category is the skill

🧰 The stack I'd learn first
Git, GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Argo CD, Prometheus and Grafana, Trivy and Vault, Backstage. One per category, learned deep. Swapping any of them out later takes a weekend, not a career.

videoTitle: The New Reality of DevOps: Code is Cheap (Deal With It)
videoDescription:
A lot of people right now are like, "Oh, I hate AI, I don't want to talk about it." I get it. I spent more than 8 years in the trenches doing DevOps, and some of the frustration is legit. But refusing to adapt is a different thing.

Writing code used to be the slow part. Now you describe what you want and get a few hundred lines back in under a minute. Code is cheap to produce, but it is not cheap to own. In this video I cover what "code is cheap" actually means, what got more expensive because of it, what the sysadmin-to-DevOps shift can teach us, and what I would do this week if I were you.

What you'll learn:
- What the Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey and the 2025 DORA report say about AI (84% use it, only 29% trust it, and delivery stability still suffers)
- Where the cost of cheap code lands: the pipeline, production, and the on-call rotation
- Why the sysadmins who kept their fundamentals ended up running platform teams
- The 5 things worth investing in now: judgment, guardrails, system design, operating everything, and clarity
- How to put guardrails on both your pipeline (policy as code, IaC scanning with Trivy) and your agent (Claude Code hooks)
- 4 things you can do this week

Sources:
- Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey: https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai
- DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development: https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/

Learn how to connect GitHub with Jenkins using webhooks and automatically deploy a static website. We also configure Slack notifications for successful and failed Jenkins builds.

videoTitle: What FinOps-Mature DevOps Leaders Do Differently (Cast AI)
videoDescription:
In this FinOps X 2026 lightning talk, Esmira Bayramova of Cast AI opens with a striking data point from analyzing 23,000+ Kubernetes clusters: only 8% of provisioned CPU, 20% of memory, and 5% of GPU actually get used.

Her core argument is that the waste isn't a cost problem, it's an ownership problem: immature teams treat cost as finance's job and review the bill retroactively once it's too late to act, while mature teams keep engineering in the room permanently, with one hard rule, no blame culture, and one real question, what did we ship per dollar?

She draws a direct line from the 2015-era "nobody thought about cloud cost until the bill exploded" story to the exact same pattern now playing out with AI and token spend, and makes the case that mature AI FinOps means tracking cost per outcome and value, not just cost per API call.

0:00 Intro: what mature DevOps leaders do differently
1:23 The reveal: 8% CPU, 20% memory, 5% GPU utilization across 23,000 clusters
2:33 Immature vs. mature: is cost finance's problem, or everyone's?
5:50 Token costs are just the new cloud waste
7:14 Cloud era vs. AI era: the metrics that actually matter

videoTitle: Build Once, Deploy Anywhere: The DevOps Standard
videoDescription:
Most teams say they have CI/CD because code moves from `dev` to `staging` to `prod`.

But if every environment rebuilds the app, the thing you tested below is not the thing running in production.

That is not promotion. That is drift with better branding.

In this video:

- how rebuild-per-environment pipelines quietly break release trust

- how to migrate to build-once, deploy-by-digest workflows
- why rollback gets dramatically cleaner when artifacts stay immutable

If production cannot prove it is running the exact artifact that passed in lower environments, the pipeline is telling a comforting story, not a trustworthy one.

videoTitle: How OpenTelemetry Tracing Actually Works

videoTitle: Observability Explained: Metrics, Logs, Traces & OpenTelemetry | DevOps Daily Dose Podcast
videoDescription:

This deep-dive audio podcast builds a complete mental model of observability: monitoring vs observability and black-box vs white-box telemetry, the three signals (metrics, logs and traces with spans), context propagation with W3C Trace Context (traceparent and tracestate) and OpenTelemetry baggage (and why you never put PII in it), the OpenTelemetry Collector's receivers, processors, exporters, memory limiter and fan-out pipelines, agent vs gateway deployment, head vs tail sampling, Jaeger v2 with direct-to-storage vs Kafka-buffered ingestion, Prometheus' pull model, service discovery and Pushgateway, PromQL instant vs range queries, classic vs native histograms and the cardinality explosion, USE, RED and the four golden signals for dashboards, SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets built on critical user journeys, Alertmanager grouping and inhibition, precision, recall, detection and reset time, and Google SRE multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting.

Who it's for: DevOps, SRE, platform and backend engineers and students, from beginners to interview level, who want to understand how telemetry flows from code to dashboards and pages, and design alerts that protect users instead of waking people up for nothing.

videoTitle: System Design Concepts Every DevOps Engineer Must Know | DevOps Daily Dose Podcast
videoDescription:
Someone hands you a dry-erase marker and says: "Design a system that handles millions of requests." Where do you even begin? This deep-dive audio podcast builds a complete mental model of system design for DevOps, the way Google SREs approach large systems with Non-Abstract Large System Design (NALSD): start with the math, then the architecture. We cover SLAs, SLOs and SLIs, five nines and error budgets, RTO and RPO, composite SLOs, monoliths 
vs microservices, API gateways, Kubernetes Services and service discovery, horizontal scaling and autoscaling (and flapping), load-balancing algorithms and cross-zone load balancing, SQL vs NoSQL, ACID vs BASE and the CAP theorem, sharding with consistent hashing, synchronous vs asynchronous replication, cache-aside and write-through caching with Redis, semantic caching, CDNs, message queues with Kafka and queue-based load leveling, CQRS, event sourcing, idempotency and the transactional outbox, plus resiliency patterns: circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting with the token bucket, load shedding, graceful degradation and exponential backoff with jitter. We finish with a full interview-style walkthrough of a 100 TB "ClickMap" system using Paxos/Raft quorums.

Who it's for: DevOps, SRE and platform engineers, cloud and backend engineers and students, from beginners to interview level, who want to understand how large systems are designed, scaled and kept reliable end to end, and who want to walk into a system design interview with a mental model instead of a list of buzzwords.

videoTitle: Pod Came Back. Why Didn't Its Files? | Kubernetes Storage
videoDescription:
Kubernetes storage explained: why a replacement Pod can be healthy while the files you saved are gone.

A container restarts, and report.pdf is still there. A deployment replaces the Pod, and the download fails. Follow the difference between emptyDir and a PersistentVolume mounted through a PersistentVolumeClaim, or PVC.

In the second run, the app saves a new report to persistent storage before another update. The replacement mounts the same volume, and the download works.

Persistent storage isn't a backup. The PVC and backing storage still need to exist and be accessible.

videoTitle: What Is Renovate / Dependabot? The Bots That Update Your Dependencies
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

What Is Renovate / Dependabot? Automated dependency update bots and why they matter for security, tested with the real Renovate 44.222.0 bot on a repo pinning two libraries from 2019.

THE PROBLEM

Two libraries in a package.json, express 4.17.1 and lodash 4.17.15. The lockfile npm builds from them pins 51 packages, written by strangers. Each one ships new versions, and some ship security advisories. Nobody tracks that by hand.

THE TWO BOTS

Dependabot comes with GitHub. Renovate is open source (AGPL-3.0) and runs on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, Gitea and more. Both read your dependency files, ask the registry what is newer, and open a pull request for each update.

MY LAB

The official renovate/renovate:44.222.0 image, run with --platform=local, which Renovate's docs say "defaults to dryRun=lookup". It plans pull requests and changes nothing. With Renovate's recommended preset it planned three.

  UPDATES 3
  BRANCH renovate/express-4.x
    express 4.17.1 to 4.22.3 minor breaking=false
  BRANCH renovate/express-5.x
    express 4.17.1 to 5.3.0 major breaking=true
  BRANCH renovate/lodash-monorepo
    lodash 4.17.15 to 4.18.1 minor breaking=false

Express 5.3.0 is a major version, flagged as breaking, so it gets its own pull request.

ONE LINE ADDED

  {
    "extends": ["config:recommended"],
    "osvVulnerabilityAlerts": true
  }

osvVulnerabilityAlerts reads vulnerability alerts from the OSV database (an experimental option, off by default). It found seven known vulnerabilities, five in lodash and two in express, three of them rated High in the GitHub Advisory Database.

  VULN GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx express 4.17.1
  VULN GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc express 4.17.1
  VULN GHSA-29mw-wpgm-hmr9 lodash 4.17.15
  VULN GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm lodash 4.17.15
  VULN GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw lodash 4.17.15
  VULN GHSA-r5fr-rjxr-66jc lodash 4.17.15
  VULN GHSA-xxjr-mmjv-4gpg lodash 4.17.15

THE FIX IS NOT THE NEWEST VERSION

  UPDATES 2
  BRANCH renovate/npm-express-vulnerability
    express 4.17.1 to 4.20.0 minor breaking=false
  BRANCH renovate/npm-lodash-vulnerability
    lodash 4.17.15 to 4.18.1 minor breaking=false

Not 5.3.0. Not even 4.22.3. Express 4.20.0, the lowest version that fixes both express advisories. In Renovate's own words, "lowest will propose the earliest version with a fix, highest will always pick the latest version." Dependabot does the same. "Then Dependabot raises a pull request to update the dependency to the minimum version that includes the patch and links the pull request to the Dependabot alert, or reports an error on the alert." A security fix should be the smallest safe jump, without dragging in a breaking change.

THE SAME JOB FOR DEPENDABOT

  version: 2
  updates:
    - package-ecosystem: "npm"
      directory: "/"
      schedule:
        interval: "weekly"
  6 lines
  schema: valid

One YAML file with a schedule, checked against the schema json.schemastore.org publishes for dependabot.yml.

THE PART THE BOTS DO NOT DO

"By default, Renovate raises PRs but leaves them to someone or something else to merge them." A pull request nobody merges patches nothing. Run your tests on every bot pull request, automerge the small ones that pass, and keep major updates for a human. Group related updates and set a schedule, so the pull requests never pile up.

Let the bot find it. Let your pipeline prove it. Then merge it fast.

videoTitle: Docker Image vs Container
videoDescription:
Image or container? They're not the same thing. Think of a recipe and the dish you cook from it.

📦 An image is the recipe: your code plus everything it needs, frozen in read-only layers. Build it once with docker build -t myapp .
▶️ A container is that image, running: docker run myapp. One image can start many containers, like a class and its objects
🗑️ Containers are throwaway: docker rm -f removes one and every change made inside it. The image stays. Keep data you need in a volume

🔍 docker images lists your images, docker ps lists running containers (docker ps -a shows stopped ones too).

Concept: Docker images vs containers.
myapp, web-1 and the status times are made-up examples.

videoTitle: Is DevOps Hard? The 3 Walls Beginners Hit, From the Hiring Side
videoDescription:
Nothing in DevOps is hard. A container is a program in a folder with rules. A pipeline is a to-do list a computer runs.
Is DevOps hard to learn? Yes, in four specific ways, and beginners hit three different walls depending on their background.

I still don't think any single piece of this work is hard. What's hard is that a hundred easy things all depend on each other, and when one breaks you don't know which layer it's in. Four specific ways it's hard, the three walls developers, sysadmins and complete switchers hit, three things beginners fear and shouldn't, and the four habits that make the difficulty manageable. No bootcamp to sell you, and no roadmap with a hundred and thirty-nine boxes on it.

Written and voiced by a Principal DevOps & Cloud Architect drawing on 17+ years of hands-on production experience across product companies, outsourcing and consultancy.

videoTitle: Run GitHub CI on Your Own Machine · Ep 29/58 #Shorts
videoDescription:
Need a GPU, a private network or your own tools in CI? Run the jobs on your own machine with a self-hosted runner. Repo Settings → Actions → Runners → New self-hosted runner shows the download and config commands (the registration token expires after one hour, so treat it like a password). Real demo: a short script gets a fresh token with the gh CLI and starts the official actions-runner image in Docker with --ephemeral and a custom label; the runner shows up Idle, a workflow with runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, docker] runs on it (the job log names the runner), and the one-job runner removes itself. Rule: keep self-hosted runners on private repos, because a fork's pull request on a public repo could run code on your machine. Larger runners are GitHub-hosted machines with more CPU, memory or a GPU, for Team and Enterprise Cloud plans, always billed per minute. Full course in order: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLdrlPUexsNwo

videoTitle: Permission Denied? chmod Explained
videoDescription:
bash: Permission denied? Your script isn't allowed to run. Here's what those rwx letters mean and how to fix it.

🔘 Every file has 3 switches: r (read), w (write), x (execute), set separately for you, your group and everyone else. ls -l shows them, like -rw-r--r--
✅ chmod +x deploy.sh turns on execute, so the script runs (usually becomes -rwxr-xr-x)
🔢 Numbers: r=4, w=2, x=1, added per group. 755 for scripts and folders, 644 for normal files

⚠️ Don't use chmod 777: it lets anyone on the machine change your file.

Concept: Unix file permissions and chmod (macOS and Linux).
deploy.sh and its output are made-up examples.

What's the last thing that gave you Permission denied? 👇

videoTitle: Pods keep changing address. How do you call one? ⚓ #kubernetes #k8s #devops
videoDescription:
Pods come and go, and every new pod has a new address. So how does anything keep calling the same one? ⚓

📞 With a Service: a phone number for your app that never changes. It gets a stable IP address and a name.
❓ It finds its pods with a selector, a label question.
✅ Call it, and your call goes to one of the pods that match and are ready.
🏠 Other pods just use its name. By default, a Service is only reachable from inside the cluster.

Part 6 of Kubernetes in a minute.

videoTitle: AWS DevOps Agent Under Pressure: Real Incident, Root Cause & Rollback
videoDescription:
A green pull request, a clean deploy, and five minutes later the shop is down. This is a real incident under real load: CloudWatch wakes AWS DevOps Agent, the agent finds the bad commit by itself, and then we hit its most important guardrail.

In this episode you will:
• Run a busy shop: a load generator inside AWS, about 100 requests per second, errors 0
• Merge a harmless-looking PR: an unbounded, query-string keyed page cache
• Watch the deploy, then the crash: 502s, OutOfMemoryError (exit 137), ECS restarting tasks
• See checkout-5xx go In alarm and start an investigation with no human click (EventBridge → webhook from episode 2)
• Watch the investigation timeline: deployments, ALB metrics, ECS health, logs and infra changes in parallel
• Read the root cause: PR #1, the exact commit and the cache line, about 10 minutes after the alarm
• Ask for a rollback in chat, read Risk details, approve, and get AccessDenied
• Learn why: changing a Fargate task definition needs iam:PassRole, and the agent's session policy never passes roles. We added the permission and retried: still denied, by design
• Apply the agent's plan yourself (Update service → revision 3) and watch errors return to 0
• Trace it in CloudTrail: the agent's calls carry the approver as sourceIdentity
• Roll forward with a Revert PR

Accuracy notes: approvals happen in the "Chat with DevOps Agent" panel; the box under an investigation re-runs it and only stages actions.

Cost: the investigation took about 10 minutes of agent time (about $5 at $0.0083 per second); chat and approvals about $1–2 more. The load generator and the ALB cost cents.

videoTitle: VM vs Contenedores: ¿Cuál deberías elegir? #tutorial #devops #programacion
videoDescription:
Máquina virtual o contenedor: la diferencia real, y por qué si usas Docker en un Mac estás usando las dos a la vez sin saberlo.

Una máquina virtual imita un ordenador completo. Un hipervisor (VMware ESXi, Proxmox, QEMU con KVM o Hyper-V) reparte el hardware real entre varias máquinas, y cada una arranca su propio sistema operativo con su propio kernel.

Un contenedor no imita nada: es un proceso más del sistema, aislado. Todos comparten el kernel de Linux del anfitrión, que los separa con dos piezas: los namespaces, para que cada uno vea solo sus propios recursos, y los cgroups, para limitar su CPU y su memoria. Docker, Podman o containerd los crean a partir de imágenes OCI por capas.

Por eso un contenedor arranca en segundos o menos, y uno de Alpine Linux no necesita más de 8 MB. El precio es el aislamiento: un fallo en el kernel compartido afecta a todos los contenedores, mientras que cada máquina virtual tiene el suyo. Por eso en la nube se combinan: los contenedores suelen ejecutarse dentro de máquinas virtuales. Y en tu Mac, Docker Desktop ejecuta el motor de Docker dentro de una máquina virtual Linux ligera.

¿Y quién decide dónde va cada contenedor cuando tienes cientos? Kubernetes. Te lo cuento en el próximo Short.

RECURSOS:
- Docker, Docker Desktop ejecuta el motor dentro de una VM Linux: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/networking/
- Linux, namespaces (man 7): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html
- Linux, cgroups (man 7): https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/cgroups.7.html
- Alpine Linux, tamaño de un contenedor: https://alpinelinux.org/about/

Logotipos de Simple Icons (CC0). Cada logotipo es marca de su propietario.

SÍGUEME:
- Web: https://antoniocintora.com

SOBRE EL CANAL:
Explico cómo funcionan por dentro las redes y la infraestructura que usamos todos los días, sin atajos y sin dar por sabido lo que no lo está. Si te interesa entender Internet de verdad, suscríbete.

¿Qué usas más en tu día a día, máquinas virtuales o contenedores? Cuéntamelo en los comentarios.

¿Qué diferencia realmente a los contenedores de las máquinas virtuales? Entiende cómo el kernel y el aislamiento definen la infraestructura.

A menudo se confunden estos conceptos, pero la distinción es técnica y profunda. Mientras que las máquinas virtuales simulan un ordenador completo con su propio sistema operativo, los contenedores son procesos aislados que comparten el mismo kernel del anfitrión. Esta diferencia cambia drásticamente cómo gestionamos los recursos y la seguridad en producción.

Para implementar esta tecnología, herramientas como Docker, Podman o Containerd utilizan namespaces para garantizar la separación de procesos. Sin embargo, esta eficiencia tiene un matiz crítico: al compartir el núcleo del sistema, un fallo en el kernel podría afectar a todos los contenedores ejecutándose en esa misma instancia.

Explico cómo funcionan por dentro la infraestructura y las redes que usamos todos los días. Si te interesa entender esto de verdad, suscríbete. ¿Qué tecnología prefieres para desplegar tus servicios? Cuéntamelo en los comentarios.

videoTitle: EP 10 · Canary Deployment Explained: How One Update Crashed 8.5 Million PCs #Shorts
videoDescription:
EP 10 · One update. About 8.5 million Windows machines crashed. And it had passed validation.

On 19 July 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike content update (a config file, not new code) passed a validator that itself had a bug, and reached Windows PCs everywhere at the same time. Think of a wedding halwai who changes only the masala, gets a thumbs-up from a taster with a cold, and serves all 500 plates at once.

The interview answer: a metric-gated canary. Serve one table first, compare its error rate and latency with the old version, then widen 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%. Metrics worse? Automatic rollback, and only one table is hurt. And yes, config changes need canaries too.

Save this for your next system design round, and comment the deploy strategy your team uses.

videoTitle: Alarms to AI: Trigger AWS DevOps Agent With EventBridge & Webhooks
videoDescription:
An alarm at 2 AM wakes a human. In this episode we make it wake AWS DevOps Agent first: a real CloudWatch alarm starts an investigation by itself, with no code, and the agent follows your own runbook.

In this episode you will:
• Build an alarm users would feel: ALB HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count, Sum over 1 minute ≥ 10, missing data as good
• Add latency (p95) and memory alarms from the CLI
• Create an Agent Space webhook with an API key, and see the incident schema it expects
• Build an EventBridge rule (Advanced builder): checkout-* alarms in ALARM → API destination with a bearer key, plus an input transformer that turns the alarm into an incident
• See the HMAC alternative: a Lambda that signs timestamp:body (we tested it: body-only signatures get a 403)
• Fire a drill with set-alarm-state and watch the investigation appear by itself, then cancel it
• Teach the agent your runbook with a custom skill
• Find the native integrations: Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty, ServiceNow, Slack, Datadog

Why not a built-in trigger? DevOps Agent's own triggers only run on schedules, so events go through the webhook.

Cost: the drill ran under two minutes of agent time (about $0.90 at $0.0083 per second). Alarms are $0.10 per month each, and the EventBridge connection secret is about $0.40 per month.
