videoTitle: Merge vs Rebase vs Squash · Ep 12/58 #Shorts
videoDescription:
Same two commits, three histories. git merge keeps every commit and adds a merge commit (the true history). git merge --squash stages the branch's changes so you commit them as one tidy commit. git rebase main replays your commits on top of main, so main fast-forwards to a straight line, but the commits get new hashes. Golden rule: never rebase commits others already have. On GitHub, Settings → Pull Requests sets which of Allow merge commits, Allow squash merging and Allow rebase merging your repo offers. Full course in order: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLeO-XlahsiKE

videoTitle: Applying DevOps Where Assumptions Break | Borislav Sabotinov | DevOpsDays Austin 2026
videoDescription:
Applying DevOps Where Assumptions Break
Borislav Sabotinov, DevOpsDays Austin 2026 (Day 1, May 5, 2026)

High-Performance Compute (HPC) environments break many assumptions behind modern DevOps and CI/CD. Simulation jobs are long-running, stateful, and expensive to fail. Feedback can arrive hours or days too late to be useful.

This talk demonstrates how applying DevOps principles in an enterprise HPC and simulation environment saves valuable time by shifting focus away from deployments and toward feedback loops. From error troubleshooting after the fact to failure prevention. Instead of forcing standard CI/CD patterns  we adapted them to fit the constraints and delivered measurable value in reduced wasted compute, faster feedback, and better outcomes for engineers.

High-Performance Compute (HPC) environments are expensive to operate in part because a sizeable chunk of engineer and compute time is "wasted" via failed jobs. Engineers submit long-running jobs, wait hours or days, and only then discover failures or unusable results. By that point, the data is stale, decisions are delayed, and compute and engineer time is lost.

This talk is a real enterprise case study in applying a DevOps mindset to HPC by identifying and exploiting the true constraint: a reactive, instead of a proactive, feedback loop. We flipped the model from post-mortem analsysis to pre-submit validation and near real-time alerts so engineers could act with immediacy on timely, relevant data.

The result was a measurable decrease in wasted compute and faster recovery time. Hundreds of thousands of compute hours preserved, tens of thousands of engineer hours saved, and millions of dollars annually avoided in wasted reruns and idle decision time. 

This talk is about how applying DevOps principles to the actual constraint, not the visible symptoms, allowed value to flow all the way down to the customer in an environment where DevOps may not even be part of the conversation.

About Borislav Sabotinov:
Boris is a software engineer based in sunny Austin, TX working on large-scale engineering platforms that span High-Performance Compute (HPC), container orchestration platforms, and cloud systems. He cares about practical DevOps, improving feedback loops, and making complex systems less frustrating for the people who use them.

videoTitle: North Korea Robbed Binance Via A DevOps Laptop
videoDescription:
0:00 The Claude Code update that wasn't Anthropic's  
3:19 The checkout that took one cent  
4:49 Six billion dollars in twenty minutes

About $6.3 billion left Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, the largest crypto theft on record. Binance points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop plus additional points of breach. TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute it to North Korea's TraderTraitor, the group behind the 2025 Bybit theft. About $2.7 billion in stablecoins was frozen; Binance says it will cover the losses. Kevin Beaumont says Binance uses Claude Code on Cursor, and the theft started inside the window when a backdoored Claude Code extension was live there; none of the companies has tied the two together.

Claude Code in Cursor: for about eleven hours on October 29, Cursor's extension marketplace served tampered versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) through Anthropic's official account there. A 66-line loader added an attacker's SSH key, tried to open a reverse SSH tunnel, set up persistence, and sent host details home. Bugs in the malware stopped the tunnel on most Mac and Windows machines, but the key and persistence stay even after you update. If you used Claude Code in Cursor that day, run Cursor's check for the svc-telemetry key and follow its remediation steps. Anthropic says its own systems weren't compromised; Cursor hasn't said how the upload happened.

Drupal: Commerce Core has an actively exploited access-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-118539) used to tamper with orders, including one-cent prices. Update to Commerce Core 3.3.13 or 8.x-2.41 and audit recent orders.

videoTitle: Claude Code Security: "Don't Ask Again" Put His API Key on GitHub
videoDescription:
A Claude Code security slip: "don't ask again" can save your command, secret and all, in .claude/settings.local.json. Apiiro found 1,122 public copies of that file holding secrets.

What to do before your next commit:
1. Rotate any key that ever sat in that file. Deleting the file does not delete it from git history or forks.
2. Add .claude/settings.local.json to your project's .gitignore. Claude Code's own exclusion only lives on one computer.
3. Share team rules in .claude/settings.json instead.
4. Deny .env: "Read(./.env)" and "Read(./.env.*)".

Sources:
https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/claude-codes-dont-ask-again-file.html

videoTitle: Prevent the Next Incident: AWS DevOps Agent Recommendations & SRE Chat
videoDescription:
The outage is fixed. Now make sure it never comes back. We rate the agent's investigation, run an on-demand evaluation, open the recommendation it writes about our own bug, switch on the fix it suggested, ask the agent a question in chat, and finish with a production checklist and a full, verified cleanup.

In this episode you will:
• Add feedback to the episode 3 investigation (Review tab: root cause correct + a note)
• Run a prevention evaluation now instead of waiting for the weekly run (Improvements · Run now)
• Read the recommendation: a pre-deploy memory load gate for the pipeline, naming our PR, commit and cache line, with next steps, trade-offs and alternatives
• Turn on the ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback, and see why the panel still says "Turned off" until a new deployment
• Ask the on-demand agent what changed in the last 3 hours and get a 5xx chart and the current error rate
• Walk through a production checklist and a multi-account reference architecture
• Delete everything on camera (Agent Space, EventBridge rule, API destination, connection, alarms, ECS service, ALB, target group) and prove it with the CLI

Cost: the evaluation took about 13 minutes of agent time (about $6 at $0.0083 per second); the chat about 4 minutes (about $2). Evaluations run weekly by default and use the same per-second price.

Accuracy notes: a deployment-configuration change alone starts no ECS deployment, so the Deployments tab keeps describing the previous deployment; force a new deployment to see "Circuit breaker: Monitoring". The circuit breaker came from the investigation's durable-fix note; the evaluation's recommendation targeted the pipeline.

videoTitle: helm install --dry-run Doesn't Check Your Cluster ⚠️ #Shorts
videoDescription:
In Helm 4, a plain --dry-run is --dry-run=client. It renders your chart on your machine and never connects to the cluster, which is basically what helm template does.

helm template → renders locally, lookup returns empty
helm install --dry-run=client → renders locally, no cluster connection
helm install --dry-run=server → talks to the cluster, so lookup sees real data (needs a reachable cluster)

Tip: helm template for quick renders. --dry-run=server before you ship.
Bonus: on Helm 4, a bare --dry-run prints a warning that it's deprecated and should be replaced with --dry-run=client.

videoTitle: The 7 DevOps Projects I’d Build to Get Hired in 2027
videoDescription:
Most DevOps portfolios look the same: a Dockerfile, a GitHub Actions workflow that runs echo hello, and a README that says "deploy to Kubernetes". That proves you can follow a tutorial. It doesn't prove you can run anything.

These are the 7 DevOps projects I'd build if I were starting over and trying to get hired in 2027. They're in order of difficulty, each one builds on the last, and you can use one boring app (a small API with a database) across all seven. By project 7, you have one system with a real history that you can talk about for an hour.

For every project, I cover two things: what it actually proves to the person interviewing you, and exactly how I'd explain it out loud in the interview.

🗳️ You pick what I build next
I'm going to build these on the channel, start to finish. Every project has a number. Drop the one you want to see first in the comments, and the one with the most votes becomes the next full build video.

📋 The 7 projects:
1. Containerize an app and ship it with CI: multi-stage Dockerfile, non-root user, pinned base image, GitHub Actions that lints, tests, builds, scans, and pushes, every image tagged with the git commit SHA
2. Build AWS with Terraform: VPC, compute, and a database, remote state in S3 with native locking, Terraform plans posted on pull requests, OIDC instead of long-lived keys
3. One push to production on Kubernetes: GitOps with Argo CD or Flux, then ship a broken release on purpose and roll back with a git revert
4. Monitoring and alerting: kube-prometheus-stack, request rate, error rate and latency, and one good alert on what users actually feel
5. Break a cluster and explain what happened: delete CoreDNS, block everything with a network policy, get pods OOMKilled, then write the postmortem
6. A self-hosted dev platform: Forgejo, Postgres, Caddy and Forgejo Runner on a mini PC, plus the day 2 work: backups, restores, upgrades, hardening
7. Run an AI agent with guardrails: read-only AWS role, human approval for destructive commands, an audit trail, and a test where the agent hits the wall

videoTitle: Git Merge vs Rebase
videoDescription:
Merge or rebase? Same code, different history.

Your feature branch has commits, and main moved on too. Here's how the two ways to bring them together actually differ.

🔀 git merge main ties the branches together with a merge commit. Nothing is rewritten.
📏 git rebase main replays your commits on top of main: one straight line, but brand-new commits with new IDs.
🤝 Rule of thumb: rebase your own branch before you push it; merge a shared branch others have pulled.

Concept: merge vs rebase (Git history)
Commit IDs shown are illustrative.

videoTitle: Your Server Clock Is Wrong! Check Your Clock ⭐ (Part 5/9) #backend #jwt #programming
videoDescription:
Edge case 2: your logs say "jwt expired", but the token is only 14 minutes old. The bug is a tiny quartz crystal.

Server clocks drift with heat, age and cheap parts. If the API server is one minute ahead of the login server, it rejects perfectly good tokens. And it works fine on your laptop, because there both run on one clock. Part 5 of 9.

videoTitle: Fix JWT Clock Skew in 2 Steps ⭐ (Part 6/9) #backend #jwt #programming
videoDescription:
Fixing JWT clock skew takes two steps. Step 1: NTP. Your server asks a time server "what time is it?", adds the travel time, and slowly corrects its clock, checking again every few minutes.

Step 2: NTP makes clocks close, not equal, so add a small grace period: clockTolerance: 30 in jwt.verify (other libraries call it leeway). 30 seconds fixes false errors; an hour would just help attackers. Part 6 of 9.

Azure Static Web Apps Complete Course · Episode 7 of 21

The Azure DevOps side follows in labelled illustrations: storing it in a secret variable group with pipeline permissions, creating the pipeline from the existing YAML file, running it and reading the run history. Azure DevOps CLI commands are typed only.

HOW THIS VIDEO WAS MADE
- Real terminal: bash in a local practice sandbox on Linux with real Node.js 22, the Azure Static Web Apps CLI 2.1, Azure Functions Core Tools 4 and Azure CLI 2.91. Every command marked as run was really run and the output is unedited.
- Illustrations: Azure portal, GitHub, Azure DevOps and Microsoft sign-in screens are faithful recreations for teaching, labelled ILLUSTRATION on screen the whole time they are shown. Nobody signed in to Azure, GitHub or Azure DevOps, and no real cloud resources were created, changed or deleted.
- Typed only: commands that need a signed-in Azure subscription were typed on screen, never run, and cancelled with Ctrl+C (marked TYPED ONLY), so no output was invented:
    az pipelines variable-group create --name swa-secrets --variables placeholder=1 --organization https://dev.azure.com/contoso-learning --project swa-demo
    az pipelines variable-group variable create --group-id 1 --name deployment_token --secret true --value YOUR_TOKEN
    az pipelines create --name swa-demo --repository swa-demo --repository-type tfsgit --branch main --yml-path azure-pipelines.yml
    az pipelines run --name swa-demo --branch main
- Key badges show the Mac keys and the Windows / Linux keys for every shortcut pressed.

NOTES ON THE COURSE SCRIPT
- Rewritten for the complete course: the Azure portal steps and the token command now run on the real portal and CLI (Free plan); Azure DevOps remains a labelled illustration.
- The pipeline in the video uses '/' and 'dist' to match the Vite project; the documentation's src/api/public sample is shown as a diff.

PRACTICE
1. Write azure-pipelines.yml for your app.
2. Create a Static Web App with source Other and store its token in a variable group.
3. Authorize the pipeline, run it and read the AzureStaticWebApp task log.

PROJECT FILES
07-project-files.zip holds the practice files exactly as they were at the end of the recording, with a README that lists every command used.

ABOUT THE SERIES
A twenty-one-part course on Azure Static Web Apps, recorded on the real Azure portal with a free Azure account: resource groups, what Static Web Apps provides, creating and deploying an app from the portal, the Azure CLI and the Static Web Apps CLI, GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps pipelines, custom domains, environments, staticwebapp.config.json, managed Azure Functions APIs and operations, then built-in Microsoft sign-in, roles and protected API routes, restricting sign-in to one Microsoft Entra tenant, creating an Azure Key Vault step by step, Key Vault fundamentals, managed identity and Key Vault references, local development with the authentication emulator, and an end-to-end secure pattern. Static Web Apps runs on the Free plan; the only paid resource is one pay-per-operation Key Vault, deleted and purged after recording. Standard-plan-only steps are shown up to the review screen without creating anything.

You'll learn how DevOps actually works: CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, GitOps, observability, incident response, DevSecOps and reliability. Then you'll get a realistic 12-month roadmap to doing this work yourself.

videoTitle: A broken version for 10 minutes. Does Kubernetes roll it back?
videoDescription:
My new version failed its readiness probe for ten minutes on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). Kubernetes rolled nothing back: kubectl only said "exceeded its progress deadline". The old pod kept serving, 718 calls and 0 failed, and both pods were still there. A stuck rollout waits. Undo is your job: kubectl rollout undo, or a pipeline that runs it.

videoTitle: How to use AWS for DevOps - 2027
videoDescription:
AWS for DevOps: IAM, Multi-Account, VPC, EKS, Pod Identity & GitHub OIDC | DevOps Basics S2E10

Most of the tools in this series run somewhere, and very often that somewhere is Amazon Web Services. Today we take a DevOps engineer’s tour of AWS.

We start with the shared responsibility model and IAM: users, roles, policies and how to apply least privilege in practice. Then we set up a multi-account organization with guardrails, design a VPC with public, private and data subnets, and control traffic with security groups and VPC endpoints. Next we compare compute options, from EC2 to ECS, EKS and Lambda, run Kubernetes on EKS with Karpenter, give pods AWS permissions with EKS Pod Identity and deploy from GitHub Actions with OIDC, without any stored keys. We finish with storage and databases, observability and audit with CloudWatch, CloudTrail and GuardDuty, Terraform on AWS, and how to keep the bill under control.
